segments: The eighteenth dynasty: the Arab kings, and his sons, and the members of his household;
and that they would confess {yield their breath}:
that these things which had happened
happened through bad counselors;
and if he would spare their lives from now on and grant them life,
they would be servants and subjects, paying tribute.
And when these men went out to the King of Kings
and fulfilled their embassy,
he detained them and did not permit them to return to the Caliph.
And he intensified the battle,
and the Tatars breached a great breach in the tower of the Persians (al-ʿAjam),
and entered the city
on Friday, the twenty-fifth of the first month (Jumada I).
And the people of the city fought bravely against them,
and drove them outside again.
And the Tatars grew strong again,
and on the following day,
that is to say, on Saturday,
they gained mastery over all the walls.
And the Baghdadites fled
and hid in the houses and subterranean vaults.
And on that same Saturday,
both sons of the Caliph went outside to the King of Kings,
and after an hour the Caliph himself also went out.
And the King of Kings gave orders,
and they put irons on him,
and guards stood over him in one of the tents for seven days,
until that King of Kings entered in person into the palace of the Caliph,
and searched the roofs, the hiding places, and the ancient and modern treasures,
and revealed all of them, and brought them out.
And the Mongols drew their swords
and slaughtered all the people of Baghdad, myriads of human beings;
especially the Iberians (Georgians) made a great slaughter.
And the Catholicos gathered all the Christians into the church of the Three Markets,
and protected them there,
and not one of the Christians was harmed.
Even the rich men among the Arabs brought the majority of their possessions to the Catholicos,
so that perhaps if they were saved, they would take what was theirs;
yet they were all killed.
Afterwards, however, when the King of Kings had recovered his composure a little,
he had the miserable Caliph brought before him,
and judged him and condemned him to death.
And he gave orders, and they put him in a sack and sewed it up over him,
and with kicks of their feet they killed him.
Because certain Arab men had frightened the King of Kings, saying:
"If any of this man's blood is shed on the earth,
rain will never descend upon it again,
and moreover coals of fire will break out from it."
And here came to an end the kingdom of the Abbasids,
as well as the rest of the kingdoms of the Arabs.
